title: Washington Civics & Government (12th Grade)
description: Washington Civics & Government (12th Grade) practice - 100 questions

questions.question: A city council votes to cancel the next election and keep its current members in office indefinitely. Which founding principle does this action attack most directly?
questions.correctAnswer: Popular sovereignty - final governing authority rests with the people
distractors: Federalism - power is divided between national and state governments
Judicial review - courts may strike down unconstitutional laws
Free enterprise - markets should operate with little regulation
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty means the people are the source of government power, exercised through elections and constitutions. A council that cancels elections keeps power the people never granted it permanently.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: If the people cannot choose, the people do not rule.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of adult citizens placing ballots into a clear ballot box outside a neoclassical city hall at dawn. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Popular sovereignty: authority comes from the people.
img.title: POWER FROM THE PEOPLE

questions.question: At a Fourth of July speech in Tacoma, a speaker argues that a king does not hand people their rights - people are born with them, and a government exists only to guard them. Which founding document gives that argument its famous list of rights?
questions.correctAnswer: The Declaration of Independence - life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
distractors: The United States Constitution - speech, religion and a fair trial
The Mayflower Compact - obedience, order and self-government
The English Petition of Right - no taxation without Parliament
questions.explanation: The speaker is echoing Thomas Jefferson's Declaration of Independence, adopted on July 4, 1776. It calls life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness unalienable rights and says governments are instituted to secure them, drawing their just powers from the consent of the governed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Born with rights - life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an outdoor speaker addressing a Fourth of July crowd in Tacoma with a bay and mountain behind, bunting overhead and listeners holding small plain flags. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Declaration names life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
img.title: BORN WITH RIGHTS

questions.question: Before stepping ashore in 1620, leaders aboard a ship signed an agreement to form a government together and to obey the laws they would make for the common good. Which founding-era idea does that agreement best illustrate?
questions.correctAnswer: The social contract - people consent to government in exchange for protection of their rights
distractors: Divine right - a ruler holds power by birth and answers only to God
Mercantilism - a colony exists to supply wealth to the mother country
Hereditary succession - office passes automatically to the ruler's eldest child
questions.explanation: The Mayflower Compact is an early American example of the social contract: people consent to create a government and follow its laws in exchange for order and protection of their rights. John Locke later gave that idea its classic form, arguing that a government that breaks the trust may be altered or replaced.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: They agreed to be governed - consent is the contract.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of passengers in 1620 clothing signing a parchment together in the cramped cabin of a wooden sailing ship, a lantern swinging above the table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Social contract: government runs on the consent of the governed.
img.title: AN AGREEMENT BEFORE ASHORE

questions.question: A county sheriff is arrested for taking bribes, and a Supreme Court justice pays a parking fine instead of having it waived as a courtesy. An editorial praises both outcomes under one heading. Which principle is it praising?
questions.correctAnswer: The rule of law - no one, not even top officials, is above the law
distractors: Separation of powers - each branch of government has a different job
Direct democracy - voters decide every government question themselves
Civilian control - elected officials command the armed forces
questions.explanation: Both officials were treated like anyone else, which is the rule of law in action: laws govern the society and apply equally to citizens and to the leaders who make and enforce them. The federal naturalization test states the same idea - everyone must follow the law, leaders included.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A badge and a robe earn no exemption from the law.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a courthouse entrance where a uniformed sheriff and a robed justice both wait in the same public line at a payment window, morning light on the steps. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Rule of law means officials obey the law too.
img.title: NO EXEMPTIONS AT THE TOP

questions.question: A city attorney stops two council plans - seizing a newspaper's presses and keeping the mayor in office past the term voters approved - by explaining that the council simply has no authority to do either. Which principle is the attorney applying?
questions.correctAnswer: Limited government - government holds only the powers the Constitution grants, and rights limit it further
distractors: Home rule - a city council may do anything its charter does not mention
Majority rule - a council majority may set aside any limit it finds inconvenient
Parliamentary supremacy - the legislature's word is final on every question
questions.explanation: The attorney is applying limited government: a government holds only the powers granted to it, must act within its constitution or charter, and is further limited by protected rights such as freedom of the press. In the American system the Constitution both grants power and fences it in.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No grant, no power - that is limited government.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a city attorney standing between a council table and a printing press, one hand raised in a stop gesture, a charter book lying open nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Limited government: power is granted, bounded and rights-checked.
img.title: NO GRANT, NO POWER

questions.question: On a museum tour, visitors stop at the opening paragraph of the Constitution, where the framers state why they are creating the government - to form a more perfect union, establish justice, insure domestic tranquility and secure the blessings of liberty. What is that paragraph called?
questions.correctAnswer: In the Preamble, the introduction to the US Constitution
distractors: The First Amendment, which lists freedoms the government may not touch
The Necessary and Proper Clause, which lets Congress choose its means
The oath of office, which every federal official swears on taking power
questions.explanation: That opening paragraph is the Preamble, the Constitution's introduction. It names six purposes for the new government, including providing for the common defense and promoting the general welfare, but it grants no power by itself - the powers come from the articles that follow.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: First paragraph, six purposes - that is the Preamble.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of museum visitors wearing headphones looking up at a large framed parchment page displayed behind glass in a quiet gallery. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The six goals of government are listed in the Preamble.
img.title: THE OPENING PARAGRAPH

questions.question: An archivist sorts three folders in constitutional order. The first holds lawmaking, taxing and war-declaring powers; the second holds command of the armed forces and execution of the laws; the third holds deciding cases that arise under federal law. Which articles created the institutions in those folders, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: Article I (Congress), Article II (the President) and Article III (the courts)
distractors: Article I (the courts), Article II (Congress) and Article III (the President)
Article V (Congress), Article VI (the President) and Article VII (the courts)
Article II (the states), Article IV (Congress) and Article I (the courts)
questions.explanation: The folders follow the Constitution's own order: Article I creates the legislative branch, Congress; Article II creates the executive branch, headed by the President; and Article III creates the judicial branch, headed by the Supreme Court. Articles IV through VII handle state relations, amendments, supremacy and ratification.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Folder one makes laws, folder two enforces, folder three decides.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an archivist placing three plain folders on shelves inside a marble records vault, a domed capitol visible through a tall window. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Articles I, II and III create Congress, the President and the courts.
img.title: THREE FOLDERS IN ORDER

questions.question: A trucking company follows a new state equipment rule that directly contradicts a valid federal safety law for interstate carriers, arguing that the state rule is newer and therefore controls. How must a court resolve the conflict?
questions.correctAnswer: The Supremacy Clause - valid federal law overrides a conflicting state law
distractors: The newer rule wins, so the state law controls until Congress updates its law
The company may pick whichever rule is cheaper for each shipment
Both rules fall, leaving interstate trucking unregulated until the states agree
questions.explanation: Article VI contains the Supremacy Clause: the Constitution, valid federal laws and treaties are the supreme law of the land. When a state law genuinely conflicts with a valid federal law, the federal law prevails no matter which was passed later.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Newer does not beat supreme - valid federal law wins a true clash.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two freight trucks stopped at a state border weigh station while an inspector compares two plain rule books under a highway gantry. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Supremacy Clause: valid federal law beats conflicting state law.
img.title: NEWER DOES NOT WIN

questions.question: An advocacy campaign celebrates after the House votes 295 to 140 and the Senate votes 68 to 32 to send a proposed constitutional change to the states, but its director warns that the celebration is early. Which statement explains her warning?
questions.correctAnswer: Proposal is finished - the amendment still needs ratification by three-fourths of the states
distractors: Ratification is finished - only the President's signature remains to make it official
Proposal is finished - a national referendum of all voters will now decide it
Nothing is finished - the change must be proposed again by a convention of governors
questions.explanation: The lopsided votes clear the first Article V hurdle: proposal by two-thirds of both houses of Congress. The amendment is not yet law - it still needs ratification by three-fourths of the states, acting through their legislatures or state conventions, and the President plays no part in either stage.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Congress proposes by two-thirds; the states still decide by three-fourths.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of legislators applauding in a large chamber while one leader holds up a cautioning hand toward a map of many state capitols on the far wall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Amendments: proposed by two-thirds of Congress, ratified by three-fourths of the states.
img.title: ONLY HALFWAY THERE

questions.question: A president nominates a judge, the Senate refuses to confirm the nominee, and the House refuses to fund a program the president wants. A commentator calls the week a breakdown of government. Which concept explains why the system deliberately allows each of those moves?
questions.correctAnswer: Checks and balances - each branch can limit the power of the others
distractors: Federalism - the states may veto any action of the national government
Direct democracy - voters must approve nominations and budgets in referendums
Unanimous consent - no branch may act until the other two agree in advance
questions.explanation: The moves are checks and balances working as designed. The Constitution separates the branches, then gives each one tools to restrain the others - the Senate's confirmation power and the House's power of the purse are two of them - so that ambition in one place is met by resistance in another.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Refusals can be the system working, not breaking.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of three large interlocking stone gears turning against one another above a capitol plaza, each gear slowing the next. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Checks and balances let each branch limit the others.
img.title: FRICTION BY DESIGN

questions.question: A textbook divides the work of government this way: one body makes laws, a separate officer enforces them, and independent judges interpret them. Which principle is the textbook describing, and where did the framers get much of the idea?
questions.correctAnswer: Separation of powers - developed by Montesquieu and built into the first three articles
distractors: Direct democracy - described by Rousseau and copied from Athens
Unitary government - developed by Hobbes and copied from England
Confederation - described by Locke and copied from the Iroquois alone
questions.explanation: Montesquieu argued that liberty survives when legislative, executive and judicial powers sit in different hands. The framers built that separation into Articles I, II and III, then added checks so the separated branches could still restrain one another.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Three jobs, three separate pairs of hands.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of three separate worktables in one hall, one with scrolls, one with a seal and one with a gavel and scales. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Separation of powers: different branches make, enforce and interpret laws.
img.title: THREE JOBS, THREE HANDS

questions.question: Only Congress may declare war and coin money, while states run elections and schools, and both levels may tax. Which system of government do these arrangements describe?
questions.correctAnswer: Federalism - power is divided between a national government and state governments
distractors: A unitary system - one central government holds all power
A confederation - states hold all power and the center only advises
A parliamentary system - the legislature chooses the chief executive
questions.explanation: In the federal system created by the Constitution, power is divided between the national government and the states. The naturalization test describes the US system the same way: a federal democratic republic under the Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two levels, each with real power of its own.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a two-story civic building with a national eagle emblem on the upper floor and a state star emblem on the lower floor, both floors lit. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Federalism divides power between national and state governments.
img.title: TWO LEVELS OF POWER

questions.question: Congress declares war, coins money and regulates trade with foreign nations, and no state may sign a treaty. Which category of power do these examples belong to?
questions.correctAnswer: Delegated (enumerated) powers - powers the Constitution grants to the federal government
distractors: Reserved powers - powers the Constitution keeps for the states
Concurrent powers - powers both levels exercise at the same time
Denied powers - powers the Constitution forbids to everyone
questions.explanation: Article I and other parts of the Constitution delegate listed powers to the national government, including declaring war, coining money and conducting foreign relations. Powers not delegated are reserved to the states or the people.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Delegated means handed over to the national government.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of state delegates handing a ring of large brass keys up the steps of a marble federal building. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Delegated powers are granted to the federal government by the Constitution.
img.title: POWERS HANDED OVER

questions.question: Washington's legislature defines most theft and assault crimes, the state runs its own prisons, and state troopers enforce speed limits on state highways - none of which the Constitution assigns to the federal government. On what basis does the state do all of this?
questions.correctAnswer: Reserved powers - the Tenth Amendment keeps undelegated powers for the states or the people
distractors: Delegated powers - Article I assigns state crimes and highways to the governor
Treaty powers - the state acts under its agreements with neighboring states
Implied powers - the Elastic Clause lets states claim any useful authority
questions.explanation: These are exercises of the state police power, held as reserved powers. The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states, or to the people, every power the Constitution does not delegate to the federal government or deny to the states - and ordinary criminal law and highway safety were never delegated away.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ordinary crimes and state roads were never handed over.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a state trooper beside a patrol car on a forested Washington highway at dusk, a county courthouse visible in the valley town below. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Reserved powers stay with the states under the Tenth Amendment.
img.title: THE STATE POLICE POWER

questions.question: A bridge over the Columbia River is financed partly with federal borrowing and partly with bonds Washington issued itself, and that same week federal courts and Washington state courts both hear cases. Which category of power explains how both levels can borrow, build roads and run courts at the same time?
questions.correctAnswer: Concurrent powers - powers the federal and state governments may exercise at the same time
distractors: Exclusive powers - borrowing and courts belong to one level of government only
Denied powers - neither level may borrow until the other gives permission
Reserved powers - borrowing and courts were left entirely to the states
questions.explanation: Borrowing money, building roads and establishing courts are concurrent powers, exercised by both levels simultaneously - as is the classic example, taxing. Coining money, by contrast, is exclusive to the federal government, which shows the line between shared and single-level powers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two levels, same toolbox - borrow, build, judge, tax.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a large bridge under construction over a wide river, work crews and cranes on both banks beneath two plain flags. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Concurrent powers, like taxing and borrowing, belong to both levels at once.
img.title: ONE BRIDGE, TWO BUILDERS

questions.question: Congress creates a national air traffic control system even though the Constitution never mentions airplanes, arguing that safe interstate air travel is needed to regulate commerce and move military aircraft. Lawyers defending the system point to the same clause the Supreme Court upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland (1819). Which clause is it?
questions.correctAnswer: The Necessary and Proper Clause - Congress may choose means to carry out its listed powers
distractors: The Tenth Amendment - it expands federal power whenever Congress finds a new technology
The Preamble - its promise of domestic tranquility grants any useful power
The Commerce Clause standing alone - it names every federal agency Congress may create
questions.explanation: The Necessary and Proper, or Elastic, Clause lets Congress choose the means for carrying out its listed powers, which creates implied powers such as chartering a bank in McCulloch or running air traffic control today. In McCulloch the Court also barred Maryland from taxing the federal bank, since a state tax could destroy a federal instrument.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: New machines, old clause - the means stretch, the ends stay listed.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an air traffic control tower guiding passenger jets and a military transport across a busy sky at dawn. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Implied powers flow from the Necessary and Proper Clause.
img.title: AIRPLANES THE FRAMERS NEVER SAW

questions.question: Merchants in 1786 complain that states are taxing each other's goods, Congress cannot pay its soldiers or make the states honor a treaty, and each state prints money of a different value. Delegates cite this chaos when calling a convention in Philadelphia. Which first plan of government produced the weak center they want to replace?
questions.correctAnswer: The Articles of Confederation - the national government was too weak to tax, enforce laws or keep order
distractors: The Virginia Plan - it gave the national government too much taxing power
The New Jersey Plan - it created a president too strong to control
The Constitution of 1787 - it let Congress enforce every law directly
questions.explanation: The chaos describes life under the Articles of Confederation, the first plan of government after independence. It kept the states sovereign and gave Congress no power to tax, regulate trade among the states or enforce its decisions - weaknesses dramatized by Shays' Rebellion and answered by the Constitution of 1787.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Thirteen moneys and no enforcement - the Articles could not hold.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of merchants in 1780s dress arguing at wagons stopped at a state border checkpoint, sacks of goods and different paper currencies on a table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Articles left the national government too weak to act.
img.title: THIRTEEN MONEYS, NO CENTER

questions.question: Which statement best explains why, in today's Congress, Wyoming and California each send two senators while California sends many more representatives than Wyoming does?
questions.correctAnswer: The Connecticut Compromise - the House by population and the Senate equal for every state
distractors: The Missouri Compromise - states enter the Union in balanced pairs with matched delegations
The Three-Fifths Compromise - House seats were counted from a fraction of the population
The Great Awakening settlement - large and small colonies divided Congress by church membership
questions.explanation: That present-day pattern is the Connecticut Compromise of 1787 still at work. Locked between the Virginia Plan (representation by population) and the New Jersey Plan (equal votes per state), the convention built both into one Congress: a House apportioned by population and a Senate of two per state.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Population in one chamber, equality in the other - Connecticut's deal lives on.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a modern capitol with two chambers side by side, one a vast curved hall of many desks and one a smaller hall of paired desks. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Connecticut Compromise: House by population, Senate equal per state.
img.title: WHY THE CHAMBERS DIFFER

questions.question: A modern Supreme Court opinion cites an essay known as Federalist No. 51, on why ambition must counteract ambition, as a guide to the Constitution's original design. That essay belongs to which collection, and who produced it?
questions.correctAnswer: The Federalist Papers - Hamilton, Madison and Jay writing as Publius
distractors: Common Sense - Thomas Paine's single pamphlet urging independence in 1776
The Anti-Federalist essays - Patrick Henry writing alone against ratification
The Virginia Statute letters - the House of Burgesses writing as a body in 1765
questions.explanation: Federalist No. 51 is one of the 85 Federalist Papers, written in 1787 and 1788 by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay under the shared pen name Publius to persuade New York to ratify the Constitution. Courts and scholars still mine the essays for the framers' understanding of the document.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Publius still gets cited - Hamilton, Madison and Jay.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a modern law library where a robed justice reads a bound volume of old essays at a long oak table, tall windows behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Federalist Papers argued for ratifying the Constitution.
img.title: STILL CITED IN COURT

questions.question: The Constitution is already ratified when the first Congress sends twelve proposed amendments to the states in 1789, ten of which are approved by 1791. Which political debt were the Federalists paying with that move?
questions.correctAnswer: The Anti-Federalists - their demand led to the Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments
distractors: A promise to the Loyalists - their seized property would be repaid in rights
A debt to the abolitionists - slavery would be phased out by amendment
A bargain with foreign creditors - trade rights would be written into the text
questions.explanation: The debt was owed to the Anti-Federalists, who had attacked the Constitution for creating a strong central government with no list of protected rights and had nearly blocked ratification. Federalists won ratification partly by promising amendments, and the ten ratified in 1791 became the Bill of Rights.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ratification was bought with a promise - the Bill of Rights was the payment.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of the first Congress in session in a modest hall, members debating over a stack of parchment pages while a clerk carries one page toward the door. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Anti-Federalist pressure produced the Bill of Rights.
img.title: THE PROMISE THAT WAS PAID

questions.question: A city bans a peaceful march, closes a newspaper that criticized it, and forbids residents from petitioning the council. Which single amendment protects all three activities the city is attacking?
questions.correctAnswer: The First Amendment - it protects speech, the press, assembly and petition
distractors: The Second Amendment - it protects the right to keep and bear arms
The Fourth Amendment - it protects against unreasonable searches
The Tenth Amendment - it reserves powers to the states
questions.explanation: The First Amendment protects five freedoms: religion, speech, the press, assembly and petition of the government. Marches, newspapers and petitions all fall inside that single amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One amendment, five freedoms - religion, speech, press, assembly, petition.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of citizens marching peacefully with plain banners while a printing press works in a shop window nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The First Amendment protects speech, press, assembly and petition.
img.title: FIVE FREEDOMS, ONE AMENDMENT

questions.question: A naturalization applicant is asked how many amendments the Constitution has and what the first ten are called. Which pair of answers is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: 27 amendments in total, and the first ten are called the Bill of Rights
distractors: 21 amendments in total, and the first ten are called the Articles
33 amendments in total, and the first ten are called the Preamble
50 amendments in total, and the first ten are called the Federalist Papers
questions.explanation: The Constitution has been amended 27 times. The first ten amendments, ratified together in 1791, are known as the Bill of Rights and mainly protect individual liberties against the federal government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 27 total - and the first ten travel as one famous bundle.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a marble archive wall with twenty-seven sealed scroll slots, the first ten grouped under one brass frame. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 27 amendments; the first ten are the Bill of Rights.
img.title: TWENTY-SEVEN AND THE FIRST TEN

questions.question: Police enter a home without a warrant, without consent and without any emergency, and seize papers to use at trial. Which amendment is the starting point for challenging the search?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fourth Amendment - it bars unreasonable searches and seizures and generally requires a warrant based on probable cause
distractors: The First Amendment - it bars the government from seizing opinions
The Seventh Amendment - it guarantees a jury in civil cases
The Ninth Amendment - it reserves unlisted rights to the people
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment protects people, houses, papers and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures. Evidence taken in serious violation of it can be excluded at trial under Mapp v. Ohio.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No warrant, no probable cause, no search.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a uniformed officer pausing at a closed front door while a judge reviews a warrant application at a desk. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Fourth Amendment guards against unreasonable searches and seizures.
img.title: THE WARRANT GUARD

questions.question: A defendant refuses to testify against herself, objects to being tried a second time for the same offense after acquittal, and objects when the government takes her land for a highway without paying her. Which amendment covers all three complaints?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fifth Amendment - self-incrimination, double jeopardy and just compensation for taken property
distractors: The Third Amendment - quartering soldiers in private homes
The Sixth Amendment - speedy trial and assistance of counsel
The Eighth Amendment - excessive bail and cruel punishments
questions.explanation: The Fifth Amendment bundles several protections: no self-incrimination, no loss of life, liberty or property without due process, grand jury indictment for serious federal crimes, no double jeopardy, and just compensation when private property is taken for public use.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fifth is a bundle - silence, fairness and payment for takings.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a courthouse scene with a silent witness, a balanced scale and a survey crew marking a highway line past a farmhouse. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Fifth covers self-incrimination, due process and takings.
img.title: SILENCE, FAIRNESS AND PAYMENT

questions.question: A man who cannot afford a lawyer is tried for a felony and convicted after defending himself. Under Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), what went wrong?
questions.correctAnswer: The state denied his Sixth Amendment right to counsel - states must provide a lawyer to defendants who cannot afford one in criminal cases
distractors: The state denied his Second Amendment right - defendants may be armed at trial
The state denied his Seventh Amendment right - felony trials require two juries
Nothing went wrong - counsel is guaranteed only in federal court
questions.explanation: The Sixth Amendment guarantees the assistance of counsel in criminal prosecutions. Gideon held that this right is fundamental and applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment, so an indigent felony defendant must be given a lawyer.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No money for a lawyer does not mean no lawyer.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a courtroom where a judge appoints a defense attorney to stand beside an accused man at the defense table. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Gideon: the Sixth Amendment requires counsel for those who cannot pay.
img.title: A LAWYER FOR EVERY ACCUSED

questions.question: A judge sets bail at an amount wildly beyond what is needed to ensure a defendant returns, then orders a punishment designed to torture. Which amendment speaks to both abuses?
questions.correctAnswer: The Eighth Amendment - it bars excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments
distractors: The Fourth Amendment - it bars all bail in serious cases
The Ninth Amendment - it bars any punishment not listed in 1791
The Eleventh Amendment - it bars states from punishing their own citizens
questions.explanation: The Eighth Amendment prohibits excessive bail, excessive fines and cruel and unusual punishments. Its language descends from the English Bill of Rights of 1689 and was carried into the federal Bill of Rights.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Bail must fit the flight risk, and punishment must stay humane.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a judge weighing a small stack of coins on a scale beside an empty, barred cell door standing open. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Eighth Amendment bars excessive bail and cruel punishments.
img.title: NO EXCESS, NO CRUELTY

questions.question: A state closes its public schools in one county rather than admit Black students, claiming the Bill of Rights limits only the federal government. Which amendment defeats the state's defense and powered Brown v. Board of Education (1954)?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fourteenth Amendment - its Equal Protection Clause binds the states
distractors: The Tenth Amendment - it reserves education to the states without limit
The Eleventh Amendment - it shields states from rights claims
The Third Amendment - it protects homes used as classrooms
questions.explanation: The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, forbids states to deny any person equal protection of the laws. Brown relied on it to hold that segregated public schools are inherently unequal, and most Bill of Rights protections reach the states through its Due Process Clause.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: After 1868, the states answer to equal protection too.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of children of different backgrounds walking together up the steps of a brick public school in morning light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Fourteenth Amendment applies equal protection against the states.
img.title: EQUAL PROTECTION BINDS STATES

questions.question: Slavery is abolished, Black men gain the vote on paper, women gain the vote, poll taxes are banned in federal elections, and 18-year-olds gain the vote. Which list matches those five changes to their amendments, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: 13th (slavery), 15th (race and voting), 19th (women), 24th (poll tax), 26th (voting age)
distractors: 12th (slavery), 14th (race and voting), 18th (women), 22nd (poll tax), 25th (voting age)
13th (slavery), 19th (race and voting), 15th (women), 26th (poll tax), 24th (voting age)
14th (slavery), 15th (race and voting), 19th (women), 23rd (poll tax), 27th (voting age)
questions.explanation: The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery, the 15th (1870) barred denying the vote by race, the 19th (1920) barred denying it by sex, the 24th (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections, and the 26th (1971) set the voting age at 18.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 13, 15, 19, 24, 26 - the expanding electorate in five steps.

questions.question: Students wear black armbands to protest a war and are suspended even though the protest caused no disruption. Under Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), how should a court rule?
questions.correctAnswer: For the students - schools may limit speech only when it substantially disrupts school work or invades others' rights
distractors: For the school - students surrender all speech rights at the schoolhouse gate
For the school - the First Amendment never applies to minors
For the students - schools may never regulate any student expression for any reason
questions.explanation: Tinker held that students do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. Silent, nondisruptive protest is protected; schools must show facts reasonably leading to substantial disruption to punish it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rights walk through the schoolhouse gate with the students.

img.tip: Tinker protects nondisruptive student speech.
img.title: RIGHTS AT THE GATE

questions.question: A theft suspect is handcuffed, driven to the station and recorded answering detectives' questions for forty minutes. The recording shows no one ever mentioned a right to remain silent or to a lawyer, and prosecutors want to play it at trial. The defense moves to suppress it, citing which case?
questions.correctAnswer: Miranda v. Arizona (1966)
distractors: Mapp v. Ohio (1961)
Gideon v. Wainwright (1963)
Terry v. Ohio (1968)
questions.explanation: The defense is invoking Miranda v. Arizona (1966), which requires warnings before custodial interrogation so that the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination is real in the station house. Statements taken from a person in custody without the warnings generally cannot be used in the prosecution's main case.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Handcuffs plus questions - warnings first, or the tape stays out.

questions.question: A naturalization applicant is asked what the economic system of the United States is and what its rule about government power is called when everyone, including leaders, must obey the law. Which pair is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: Capitalist (free market) economy - and the rule of law
distractors: Command economy - and the rule of law
Capitalist (free market) economy - and the spoils system
Mixed feudal economy - and the divine right of kings
questions.explanation: The naturalization test teaches that the United States has a capitalist, free market economy, and that the rule of law means everyone - citizens and leaders alike - must follow the law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Free market economy, and no one above the law.

img.tip: US economy: capitalist free market. Everyone obeys the law.

questions.question: A quiz asks: how many US senators are there, how long is one Senate term, and how often is about a third of the Senate chosen?
questions.correctAnswer: 100 senators; six-year terms; about a third elected every two years
distractors: 50 senators; four-year terms; half elected every two years
100 senators; two-year terms; all elected every two years
435 senators; six-year terms; about a third elected every four years
questions.explanation: Each state elects two senators, so the Senate has 100 members. Senators serve staggered six-year terms, with roughly one third of the seats up for election every two years, which keeps the Senate a continuing body.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two per state, six-year terms, a third at a time.

questions.question: Washington's redistricting commission redraws the state's congressional district lines after each census, because the state's share of the 435 House seats can rise or fall - yet the commission has no power to change the two United States senators the state sends. Why the difference?
questions.correctAnswer: House seats are apportioned among the states by population; Senate seats are fixed at two per state
distractors: House members face voters more often, so their number must be recalculated
The President reapportions senators, leaving only the House to the states
Senators are apportioned by land area, which the census does not measure
questions.explanation: The decennial census drives reapportionment of the House, whose seats are divided among the states by population, so a state that grows more slowly than others can lose a seat. Senate representation never moves with population - two per state was the equal-state half of the Connecticut Compromise.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Districts get redrawn; the two senators stay put.

img.tip: House seats follow population; Senate seats stay at two per state.
img.title: REDRAWING LINES, NOT SENATORS

questions.question: A naturalization applicant is asked how many voting members the House of Representatives has and how long representatives serve. Which answer is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: 435 voting members, each serving a two-year term
distractors: 100 voting members, each serving a six-year term
535 voting members, each serving a four-year term
50 voting members, each serving a one-year term
questions.explanation: The House has 435 voting members, a size set by law, and every representative serves a two-year term - the whole House is elected every two years, making it the chamber closest to the voters.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 435 seats, two-year terms - the whole House, every cycle.

img.tip: House: 435 voting members, two-year terms.

questions.question: A president is elected in November, takes office the following January, and may be reelected only once. Which pair of rules produces that limit and schedule?
questions.correctAnswer: Four-year terms set by Article II, with the 22nd Amendment capping a president at two elected terms
distractors: Six-year terms set by Article II, with the 12th Amendment capping a president at two terms
Four-year terms set by statute, with no constitutional limit on reelection
Life tenure set by Article II, ended only by impeachment
questions.explanation: Article II sets a four-year presidential term. The 22nd Amendment, ratified in 1951 after Franklin Roosevelt's four elections, limits a president to two elected terms. Presidential elections fall in November and inauguration follows on January 20.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Four years a term, two terms at most.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an inauguration platform in winter with two calendar pages and a folded flag in the foreground. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Presidents serve four-year terms, limited to two by the 22nd Amendment.
img.title: FOUR YEARS, TWICE AT MOST

questions.question: The President dies in office with two years left in the term. A classmate asks who becomes President and whether anyone must approve the choice. Which answer is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: The Vice President becomes President automatically - no election or confirmation is needed
distractors: The Secretary of State becomes President after a Senate vote
The Speaker becomes President only if Congress approves
The Chief Justice serves as acting President until a special election
questions.explanation: Under the 25th Amendment and the original succession rule, the Vice President becomes President when the office falls vacant - not merely an acting stand-in. Voters chose that successor when they elected the ticket.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Vice President steps up automatically - that is the job.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an empty presidential desk chair with a second chair beside it, flags standing behind both. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Vice President becomes President if the office falls vacant.
img.title: THE VICE PRESIDENT STEPS UP

questions.question: In one week, a president orders forces to respond to an attack, pardons a prisoner, and proposes legislation in an address to Congress. Which set of roles covers all three acts?
questions.correctAnswer: Commander in chief, chief executive (enforcing laws and granting pardons), and legislative leader
distractors: Chief justice, chief diplomat, and head of the state governments
Head of the Senate, head of the courts, and commander of state militias
Party leader only - all three acts are campaign functions
questions.explanation: The President wears several hats: commander in chief of the armed forces, chief executive who faithfully executes the laws and may grant pardons, and a legislative leader who recommends measures to Congress in the State of the Union.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One president, several hats - military, executive, legislative.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a desk with a military cap, a fountain pen and a rolled address scroll arranged in a row, flags behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The President is commander in chief and chief executive.
img.title: MANY HATS, ONE PRESIDENT

questions.question: A president calls together the heads of the executive departments - State, Treasury, Defense, Justice and the others - for advice on a crisis. What is this group, and how do its members get their jobs?
questions.correctAnswer: The Cabinet - appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate
distractors: The Joint Chiefs - elected by the armed services every four years
The federal bench - appointed by the Chief Justice
The Electoral College - chosen by state legislatures
questions.explanation: The Cabinet consists of the heads of the executive departments. The President appoints them and the Senate confirms them; they run their departments and advise the President, and they serve at the President's pleasure.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Cabinet is the President's confirmed team of department heads.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a long oval table with department heads in discussion and the President listening at the head. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Cabinet members are appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate.
img.title: THE PRESIDENT'S TEAM

questions.question: After Congress refuses to fund a new program, a president signs an order creating the program anyway and directs the Treasury to pay for it out of general funds. A court blocks the spending. Which statement best explains the court's ruling?
questions.correctAnswer: Executive orders direct the executive branch under the Constitution or existing law; they cannot create new law or spend money Congress has not appropriated
distractors: Executive orders become statutes once signed, so only a constitutional amendment can block one
A president may spend unappropriated money whenever Congress is out of session
Courts may never review an executive order, so the block must have come from the Senate
questions.explanation: An executive order is only a directive within the executive branch, valid when it rests on the Constitution or on a statute Congress has passed. It cannot create a new program of law by itself or spend money Congress has not appropriated - the power of the purse belongs to Congress - so the spending order exceeded the president's authority.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No appropriation, no spending - an order cannot open the Treasury.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a judge's gavel resting on a desk beside a funding document and a locked treasury door, a domed capitol in the distance. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Executive orders work under existing law; they are not new law.
img.title: AN ORDER CANNOT OPEN THE TREASURY

questions.question: On a White House tour, a guide is asked what can happen to a bill after both chambers pass it in identical form and send it to the president - including the outcomes if the president simply does nothing. Which answer should the guide give?
questions.correctAnswer: The President can sign it, veto it, let it become law without signing while Congress is in session, or pocket-veto it if Congress adjourns in the window
distractors: The president could have edited out the sections he disliked and signed the rest into law
The Chief Justice could have signed it whenever the president was traveling
The bill could have bypassed the president entirely and gone to the states for approval
questions.explanation: At presentment the president has four real paths: sign the bill, veto it, let it become law after ten days without a signature while Congress remains in session, or kill it by pocket veto - holding it unsigned when Congress adjourns within the ten-day window. There is no federal line-item veto; the Supreme Court struck that device down.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sign, veto, wait it into law, or pocket it - nothing is also a choice.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a tour group looking at a replica presidential desk in a museum hall, a calendar and a document resting on the desk. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A bill can be signed, vetoed, left unsigned into law, or pocket-vetoed.
img.title: NOTHING IS ALSO A CHOICE

questions.question: A bill becomes law even though the president formally returned it with objections, and it carries no presidential signature and no court order made it law. Only one constitutional path explains the outcome. Which path is it?
questions.correctAnswer: Two-thirds of both the House and the Senate voted to override the veto
distractors: The Supreme Court reversed the president's objections as unconstitutional
Three-fourths of the state legislatures voted the bill into law
The Vice President broke a tie in the Senate to enact the bill over the objection
questions.explanation: The path is a veto override: after a veto, the bill returns to Congress, and if two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate vote for it anyway, it becomes law word for word without the president's signature. The steep threshold is why overrides succeed only rarely.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Returned with objections, enacted anyway - two-thirds did it.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a packed legislative chamber with members rising to be counted, a returned bill with a red ribbon lying on the clerk's desk in the foreground. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Congress overrides a veto with two-thirds of both houses.
img.title: ENACTED WITHOUT A SIGNATURE

questions.question: A president negotiates a nuclear arms treaty and nominates a judge to a federal appeals court, but neither can take effect until the Senate acts - the treaty needing a two-thirds vote and the judge a majority. Which constitutional power is the Senate exercising in both cases?
questions.correctAnswer: Advice and consent - the Senate must approve treaties and presidential appointments
distractors: Impeachment - the Senate is deciding whether to remove both from office
Origination - treaties and nominations must both begin as Senate bills
Judicial review - the Senate is ruling both matters unconstitutional
questions.explanation: Both actions run through the Senate's advice and consent power in Article II. The president makes treaties and appointments, but treaties require approval by two-thirds of the senators present and major appointments, including judges and ambassadors, require Senate confirmation by majority vote.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Negotiate and nominate up front; consent happens in the Senate.

img.tip: Treaties and appointments need the Senate's advice and consent.

questions.question: After the House impeaches a president, supporters of removal argue that the Senate can finish the job the same way the House started it - by a simple majority. Which statement corrects them?
questions.correctAnswer: Impeachment - the House brings charges and two-thirds of the Senate convicts and removes
distractors: A recall - voters sign petitions and a simple majority of voters removes the president
A censure - the House alone may expel the president on a two-thirds vote
An indictment - a grand jury brings the charges and the Chief Justice removes
questions.explanation: The two stages use different thresholds. The House impeaches - brings the charges - by majority vote, but the Senate then conducts the trial, with the Chief Justice presiding when the president is tried, and removal requires conviction by two-thirds of the Senate. A simple Senate majority is not enough.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Majority to accuse, two-thirds to remove - the bar rises at trial.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a solemn Senate chamber arranged as a courtroom, the Chief Justice presiding from the front while senators sit as jurors in rows. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: House impeaches; two-thirds of the Senate convicts and removes.
img.title: THE BAR RISES AT TRIAL

questions.question: A new federal income tax proposal is filed in the House, passes there, and then the Senate rewrites its rates extensively before passing its own version. A senator explains that the Senate rewrite is allowed, but the original filing could not have started in the Senate. Which rule explains both halves of that statement?
questions.correctAnswer: The Origination Clause - bills for raising revenue must begin in the House of Representatives
distractors: The Commerce Clause - all money measures begin with the President's budget office
The Presentment Clause - tax bills must begin in a conference committee
The Tenth Amendment - tax bills must begin in the state capitols
questions.explanation: The Origination Clause in Article I requires bills for raising revenue to begin in the House, the chamber elected directly by the people every two years, while expressly allowing the Senate to propose amendments - which is why the Senate could rewrite the rates but could not have filed the tax bill first. Other kinds of bills may start in either chamber.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Filed in the House, freely amended in the Senate - that is origination.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a thick folder passing through an arched doorway from a large chamber toward a smaller chamber, a plain coin emblem on the folder cover. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Revenue bills must begin in the House.
img.title: FILED HERE, AMENDED THERE

questions.question: A new bill is given a number, debated in committee, amended on the floor, and passed by one chamber, then repeated through the other chamber before going to the President. Why does the system force a bill through so many steps in both chambers?
questions.correctAnswer: Bicameral passage in identical form, plus presentment, slows lawmaking so majorities must build agreement in two differently chosen bodies
distractors: The steps exist so the Supreme Court can edit bills before passage
The steps exist because the Senate may pass a different text and the President merges them
The steps are ceremonial - a bill becomes law whenever one chamber passes it
questions.explanation: The Constitution requires both houses to pass the same text and present it to the President. Committees screen, floors debate and amend, and the two chambers - one by population with two-year terms, one equal per state with six-year terms - must agree before anything becomes law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two chambers, one identical text, then the President.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a document traveling along a long table past committee chairs toward two chamber doors and a distant executive desk. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Both houses must pass the identical bill before presentment.
img.title: TWO CHAMBERS, ONE TEXT

questions.question: A would-be justice of the peace, appointed by outgoing President John Adams in his final days in office, sues over a commission that was signed but never delivered, and the Supreme Court uses the small dispute to claim a very large power. Which case is this, and what power did it establish?
questions.correctAnswer: Marbury v. Madison (1803) - judicial review, the power to strike down laws that violate the Constitution
distractors: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) - the power of Congress to charter a bank
Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) - federal control of interstate commerce
Brown v. Board of Education (1954) - the end of school segregation
questions.explanation: In Marbury v. Madison, Chief Justice John Marshall held that a section of the Judiciary Act conflicted with the Constitution and was void. It is the foundational case for judicial review, the courts' power to declare acts of the other branches unconstitutional.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A small commission case built the biggest judicial power.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a robed chief justice holding a small sealed commission beside a tall columned courthouse. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Marbury v. Madison established judicial review.
img.title: SMALL CASE, BIG POWER

questions.question: A naturalization applicant is asked what the judicial branch does and which court is the highest in the country. Which answer is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: The judicial branch reviews and explains laws, resolves disputes and decides whether a law goes against the Constitution - and the Supreme Court is the highest court
distractors: The judicial branch writes laws and commands the armed forces - and the district courts are the highest
The judicial branch enforces laws and runs elections - and the court of appeals is the highest
The judicial branch negotiates treaties and confirms judges - and state supreme courts are the highest
questions.explanation: The naturalization test sums up the judicial branch as reviewing laws, resolving disputes and deciding whether laws conflict with the Constitution. The Supreme Court sits at the top of the federal system, and its decisions are final on federal law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Courts review laws - and the Supreme Court has the last word.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of three courthouse buildings rising in tiers with the tallest columned building at the top under one flag. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States.
img.title: THE LAST WORD ON LAW

questions.question: Federal judges hold their seats for life during good behavior, and their salaries cannot be cut while they serve. Why did the framers protect judges this way?
questions.correctAnswer: To insulate judges from political pressure so they can rule against powerful officials and popular majorities when the Constitution requires it
distractors: To make judges more powerful than the elected branches in all matters
To save money by avoiding judicial elections
To let judges write laws without interference from Congress
questions.explanation: Article III gives federal judges life tenure and salary protection so their decisions rest on law rather than on pleasing voters, presidents or legislators. The check on judges is impeachment, not retaliation at the next election or in the next budget.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Life tenure buys independence, not power for its own sake.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a judge's bench carved from a single oak beam with a gavel resting beside a closed law book. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Life tenure and protected salaries keep judges independent.
img.title: INDEPENDENCE BY DESIGN

questions.question: A case begins in a federal district court, the loser appeals, and the Supreme Court eventually takes it. How did the case reach the top, and how many justices will decide it?
questions.correctAnswer: By appeal through the court of appeals and a grant of review - and nine justices sit on the Supreme Court
distractors: By direct election of the case by voters - and seven justices sit on the Supreme Court
By appointment of the case by the President - and eleven justices sit on the Supreme Court
By order of the state governor - and the number of justices changes every year
questions.explanation: Federal cases usually start in a district court (the trial court), move to a court of appeals, and reach the Supreme Court only if the justices agree to hear them. The Court has nine justices - one chief justice and eight associates - a number set by Congress, not by the Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: District, appeals, then the top - and nine chairs at the bench.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a staircase climbing past three courthouse doors to a bench with nine high-backed chairs. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Nine justices sit on the Supreme Court; Congress set the number.
img.title: NINE CHAIRS AT THE TOP

questions.question: New York grants one company a monopoly on steamboat routes that cross into New Jersey, while a rival holds a federal license for the same waters. In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824), what did the Court hold?
questions.correctAnswer: Congress's commerce power covers navigation between states, so the federal license prevails over the state monopoly
distractors: States may monopolize any trade that touches their own ports
Commerce means only the buying and selling of goods, never transportation
The federal government may license ships only on the open ocean
questions.explanation: Gibbons v. Ogden read the Commerce Clause broadly: commerce includes navigation, and Congress's power over commerce among the states overrides a conflicting state monopoly. The case anchored a wide federal role in the national economy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Commerce among the states belongs to Congress - boats included.

img.tip: Gibbons: federal commerce power covers interstate navigation.
img.title: COMMERCE CROSSES THE RIVER

questions.question: A robbery suspect is tried in state court while a separate counterfeiting case is tried in federal court, and a classmate insists one of the trials must be in the wrong building. Why is he wrong?
questions.correctAnswer: The United States has a dual court system - federal courts and state courts each hear cases under their own jurisdiction
distractors: All criminal cases must be tried in federal court by the Constitution
State courts exist only to hear appeals from federal courts
Federal courts hear only cases between foreign governments
questions.explanation: Federalism produces two court systems. Federal courts hear cases under federal law, the Constitution, treaties and disputes the Constitution assigns them; state courts hear the great majority of cases, including most crimes, contracts and family matters.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two systems of courts, each with its own cases.

img.tip: State and federal courts form a dual court system.
img.title: TWO SYSTEMS OF COURTS

questions.question: A naturalization applicant is asked to name one power that belongs only to the federal government and one that belongs only to the states. Which pairing matches the test's expected answers?
questions.correctAnswer: Federal: print money (also declare war, create an army, make treaties). State: provide police and schools (also issue licenses and approve zoning)
distractors: Federal: provide police and schools. State: print money and declare war
Federal: issue driver's licenses. State: create an army and make treaties
Federal: approve local zoning. State: coin money and set immigration law
questions.explanation: The civics test divides examples cleanly: the federal government prints money, declares war, creates an army and makes treaties. The states provide schooling and police protection, give licenses and approve zoning and land use.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Money and war up top; schools and police at the state level.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a mint press and a flag on one side of a plaza facing a schoolhouse and a police station on the other. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Federal powers: money, war, army, treaties. State powers: schools, police, licenses.
img.title: WHO DOES WHAT

questions.question: Two candidates finish a presidential election with the national popular vote nearly tied, yet one wins clearly. Which institution actually elects the President, and what number wins it?
questions.correctAnswer: The Electoral College - a candidate needs 270 of the 538 electoral votes
distractors: The House of Representatives - a candidate needs 218 of 435 votes in every election
The Senate - a candidate needs 51 of 100 votes in every election
The Supreme Court - a candidate needs 5 of 9 votes in every election
questions.explanation: Presidents are chosen by electors: each state gets electors equal to its senators plus representatives, plus three for the District of Columbia under the 23rd Amendment, for 538 total. Winning at least 270 electoral votes wins the presidency, which is why the popular vote and the outcome can differ.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 270 is the number that makes a president.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a large map of states with piles of gold tokens stacked beside each one, a finish line drawn across the middle. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: 270 of 538 electoral votes elects the President.
img.title: TWO HUNDRED SEVENTY WINS

questions.question: If no candidate wins a majority of electoral votes, a very different body chooses the President. Which body, and how does it vote?
questions.correctAnswer: The House of Representatives, voting by state delegation - each state casts one vote
distractors: The Senate, voting by state delegation - each state casts one vote
The Supreme Court, voting by seniority - each justice casts one vote
The state governors, voting by region - each region casts one vote
questions.explanation: The 12th Amendment sends a deadlocked presidential election to the House, where each state delegation casts a single vote and a majority of states wins. The Senate separately chooses the Vice President in that situation, voting per senator.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No electoral majority sends the choice to the House, one vote per state.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a chamber where legislators cluster in fifty small state groups, each group raising a single card. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The House picks the President by state delegation if electors deadlock.
img.title: ONE VOTE PER STATE

questions.question: A political party writes a platform, recruits candidates, raises money and organizes volunteers, while a single-issue group only pressures whoever wins. What is the core difference between the two organizations?
questions.correctAnswer: Parties try to win elections and run the government; interest groups try to influence policy without running candidates of their own
distractors: Parties exist only in election years; interest groups exist all the time
Parties are banned from policy debates; interest groups write the laws
Parties represent one issue; interest groups represent all issues
questions.explanation: Political parties are linkage institutions whose main job is winning office: they nominate candidates and organize government. Interest groups pursue policy goals by lobbying, research and public campaigns, but they do not nominate candidates under their own label.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Parties run for power; groups push for policy.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a convention hall with candidate podiums on one side and a row of advocacy booths along the wall on the other. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Parties seek office; interest groups seek influence.
img.title: OFFICE VERSUS INFLUENCE

questions.question: A naturalization applicant is asked to name the two major political parties in the United States today. Which answer is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: The Democratic Party and the Republican Party
distractors: The Federalist Party and the Democratic-Republican Party
The Whig Party and the Know-Nothing Party
The Liberal Party and the Conservative Party
questions.explanation: The two major parties on the naturalization test are the Democratic and Republican parties. Single-member districts and plurality elections make it hard for third parties to win office, though third parties still shape debates and sometimes outcomes.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Democrats and Republicans are the two major parties.
