img.tip: The two major parties are Democratic and Republican.
img.title: THE TWO MAJOR PARTIES

questions.question: A news outlet investigates a mayor's contracts, publishes what it finds, and public pressure forces an official inquiry. Which role of the media is on display?
questions.correctAnswer: The watchdog role - the press monitors government and exposes wrongdoing
distractors: The gatekeeper role - the press decides which candidates may run
The scorekeeper role - the press counts the official votes
The agenda role - the press writes the city's budget
questions.explanation: A free press serves as a watchdog between citizens and government: it investigates, publicizes misconduct and forces officials to answer in public. That checking role is one reason the First Amendment protects the press.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The press watches the powerful so citizens do not have to guess.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a reporter with a notebook and camera standing outside a city hall records office, sunlight through tall windows. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The watchdog press investigates and exposes wrongdoing.
img.title: THE WATCHDOG PRESS

questions.question: Every issue a newsroom covers pushes some other issue off the front page, and the topics the media emphasize become the topics voters say matter most. Which media power explains that pattern?
questions.correctAnswer: Agenda-setting - heavy coverage tells the public which issues to think about
distractors: Framing alone - word choice decides every voter's final choice
Censorship - the government approves the front page in advance
Equal time - every issue must receive identical coverage by law
questions.explanation: News organizations set the public agenda by choosing what to cover prominently and repeatedly. Voters tend to rank heavily covered issues as most important, which gives editors and producers real influence over political debate.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Coverage decides what the country argues about.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a newsroom wall of glowing screens with one large story board in the center and smaller boards dimmed at the edges. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Agenda-setting: coverage signals which issues matter.
img.title: WHAT GETS COVERED COUNTS

questions.question: A poll claims a challenger leads by 20 points, but the pollster only called landlines during weekday mornings and asked loaded questions. Why should a careful reader distrust the result?
questions.correctAnswer: The sample was not representative and the wording was biased - a scientific poll needs a random, representative sample and neutral questions
distractors: All polls are illegal before an election, so the result cannot be real
Polls must survey every voter in the state to mean anything
A 20-point lead is mathematically impossible in any election
questions.explanation: Scientific polling depends on random sampling so every voter has a known chance of being chosen, a sample that mirrors the electorate, and neutrally worded questions. Skewed samples and push-poll wording produce numbers that describe the method, not the public.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Bad samples and loaded words make bad numbers.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a researcher at a desk with a phone list crossed out and a balanced chart of many kinds of households beside it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Trust polls with random samples and neutral wording.
img.title: RANDOM SAMPLE, NEUTRAL WORDS

questions.question: A baby is born in Seattle to parents visiting from another country, and a classmate insists the baby cannot be a US citizen. Under the Fourteenth Amendment, who is right?
questions.correctAnswer: The baby is a US citizen - the Amendment grants citizenship to all persons born or naturalized in the United States
distractors: The classmate - citizenship passes only through citizen parents
The baby is a citizen only if Congress approves the birth
The baby becomes a citizen automatically at age 18
questions.explanation: The Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship Clause makes anyone born on US soil and subject to its jurisdiction a citizen, overturning the Dred Scott holding that Black Americans could not be citizens. Naturalization is the second path the clause names.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Born here means citizen here - that is the clause.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a hospital window at dawn with a newborn nursery and a city skyline of cranes and bridges behind it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Birth on US soil confers citizenship under the 14th Amendment.
img.title: BORN HERE, CITIZEN HERE

questions.question: An immigrant has been a lawful permanent resident for five years, reads and writes English, knows US civics, and has good moral character. What final steps turn a resident into a citizen?
questions.correctAnswer: Naturalization - applying, being interviewed and tested, and taking the Oath of Allegiance
distractors: Registration - signing a voter roll at the county office
Sponsorship - being claimed by a citizen employer
Residency alone - the five years complete the process automatically
questions.explanation: Naturalization is the legal process by which an immigrant becomes a citizen: an application, biometrics, an interview with English and civics tests, and the Oath of Allegiance, in which the new citizen renounces foreign allegiances and swears to support the Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Application, interview, civics test, then the oath.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a row of new citizens standing with raised right hands in a courthouse hall, small flags on every chair. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Naturalization ends with the Oath of Allegiance.
img.title: THE OATH COMPLETES IT

questions.question: A naturalization applicant is asked for one responsibility that belongs only to US citizens, as opposed to everyone living in the country. Which answer fits?
questions.correctAnswer: Serve on a jury and vote in federal elections - both are citizen-only
distractors: Obey the law and pay taxes - both are citizen-only
Get a driver's license and own property - both are citizen-only
Attend school and hold a job - both are citizen-only
questions.explanation: Everyone in the United States must obey the law and pay taxes, citizen or not. Jury service and voting in federal elections are reserved to citizens, and the naturalization test lists them as the two citizen-only responsibilities.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Obeying and paying are for everyone; juries and federal votes are for citizens.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a jury box of citizens on one side of a courtroom and a voting booth line visible through the window. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Jury service and federal voting are citizen-only responsibilities.
img.title: CITIZENS ONLY: JURIES AND VOTES

questions.question: A state tries to require voters to be 21, pay a poll tax, and pass a literacy test in federal elections. Which combination of constitutional change and law dismantled rules like these?
questions.correctAnswer: The 15th, 19th, 24th and 26th Amendments plus the Voting Rights Act of 1965 - barring denial of the vote by race and by sex, banning poll taxes in federal elections, lowering the voting age to 18, and banning literacy tests
distractors: The 12th and 22nd Amendments plus the Federalist Papers
The 9th and 10th Amendments plus a presidential proclamation
The 2nd and 3rd Amendments plus the Judiciary Act of 1789
questions.explanation: Suffrage expanded by amendment - race (15th), sex (19th), poll taxes (24th), age 18 (26th) - and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 enforced the promise by suspending literacy tests and requiring federal review of election changes in covered jurisdictions.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Amendments promised it; the Voting Rights Act enforced it.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of voters of many generations standing in one line outside a polling place at sunrise. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 banned literacy tests.
img.title: PROMISE PLUS ENFORCEMENT

questions.question: A president directs the Federal Aviation Administration to rewrite safety rules, the Environmental Protection Agency to enforce clean-air law, and the Treasury to collect taxes. Which part of government is doing this daily governing?
questions.correctAnswer: The executive branch's departments and agencies - the federal bureaucracy that carries out the laws
distractors: The federal judiciary - judges who write safety and tax rules
Congressional committees - members who collect taxes and inspect planes
State governments - governors who run federal programs directly
questions.explanation: Most federal law reaches daily life through the executive departments and agencies Congress creates and funds. Their rule-making must stay inside the statutes that authorize them, and both Congress (through oversight and funding) and the courts (through review) check them.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Agencies turn statutes into daily rules - inside the law's limits.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a wide government building with many office windows lit, inspectors and clerks moving between desks and filing shelves. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Departments and agencies carry out the laws day to day.
img.title: WHERE LAWS MEET DAILY LIFE

questions.question: Congress cuts an agency's budget to zero for one program and holds televised hearings into another agency's failures. Which congressional tool is at work in both cases?
questions.correctAnswer: Oversight - Congress checks the executive branch through funding, hearings and investigations
distractors: Judicial review - Congress strikes down agency rules as a court
Pardon power - Congress forgives the agency's officials
Ratification - Congress approves the agency's treaties
questions.explanation: Congressional oversight - hearings, investigations, reporting requirements and the power of the purse - is how the legislative branch supervises the bureaucracy between elections. Refusing to fund a program is the bluntest version of the same tool.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Hearings and the budget are Congress's leash on agencies.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a hearing room with legislators behind a long dais questioning seated agency officials, cameras along the wall. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Oversight: hearings, investigations and funding control.
img.title: HEARINGS AND THE PURSE

questions.question: Two states argue over a river boundary, and the Constitution sends their dispute straight to one court rather than up through the trial courts. Which court, and why?
questions.correctAnswer: The Supreme Court, exercising original jurisdiction - cases involving states begin there
distractors: A federal district court, exercising appellate jurisdiction over the states
The court of appeals, because state disputes are always appeals
An international court, because rivers are governed by treaty alone
questions.explanation: Article III gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in cases affecting ambassadors and those in which a state is a party, so state-versus-state suits start and end there. Nearly everything else arrives by appeal, which is the Court's appellate jurisdiction.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: State against state goes straight to the top court.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two state capitol domes on opposite banks of a wide river with a single marble courthouse on a bridge between them. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Supreme Court hears state-versus-state cases first.
img.title: STRAIGHT TO THE TOP

questions.question: A governor commands the state National Guard during a flood, but the President later federalizes the same units for overseas duty. What does the switch illustrate?
questions.correctAnswer: Dual status under federalism - the Guard serves the governor in state service and the President when called into federal service
distractors: A violation of the Third Amendment by both officials
The end of the state militia system under the 27th Amendment
A recall election triggered automatically by the deployment
questions.explanation: The National Guard is the modern form of the state militia the Constitution divides between state and federal control. Governors command it for state emergencies; the President may call it into federal service, and the chain of command follows the status.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Same soldiers, two possible commanders - status decides.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of rescue boats and uniformed guard members helping residents during a flooded street, a state flag and a national flag on two poles. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Guard answers to the governor at home, the President when federalized.
img.title: TWO COMMANDERS, ONE GUARD

questions.question: A citizen wants to influence a bill: she testifies at a hearing, joins a group that lobbies, writes her representative and campaigns in the primary. Which statement best describes what she is using?
questions.correctAnswer: Linkage institutions and participation channels - parties, groups, media and elections connect citizens to government between and during campaigns
distractors: Reserved powers - citizens hold the Tenth Amendment powers personally
Judicial review - citizens may strike down bills they oppose
Executive privilege - citizens may attend all government meetings by right
questions.explanation: Political scientists call parties, interest groups, elections and the media linkage institutions because they connect people's preferences to government action. Participation runs wider than voting: testifying, lobbying, contacting officials and campaigning all push preferences into the system.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Voting is one channel - hearings, groups and campaigns are others.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a citizen speaking at a hearing microphone while neighbors with plain signs and clipboards wait their turn. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Citizens influence government through many channels beyond voting.
img.title: MORE CHANNELS THAN VOTING

questions.question: An incumbent representative wins easily year after year: the district was drawn to favor her party, she raises far more money, and local coverage treats her as the default. Which set of advantages explains her streak?
questions.correctAnswer: Incumbency advantages - favorable district lines (gerrymandering), fundraising strength and name recognition
distractors: Term limits - the Constitution bars challengers from running
The 17th Amendment - it assigns House seats by seniority
Closed primaries alone - only incumbents may enter them
questions.explanation: Incumbents start with name recognition, donor networks, staff and a record they can campaign on, and districts drawn by the party in power (gerrymandering) can lock in those advantages. The Constitution sets no House term limits, so the advantage compounds until voters or a primary end it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Recognition, money and drawn lines - the incumbent's three walls.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a map with one district outlined in a winding ribbon shape, a campaign office window full of posters beside it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Incumbency brings recognition, money and often favorable lines.
img.title: THE INCUMBENT'S THREE WALLS

questions.question: A PAC pools contributions and gives them to candidates, a super PAC raises unlimited sums for independent ads, and a lobbyist meets a legislator to argue a bill. Which statement sorts the three correctly?
questions.correctAnswer: PACs donate limited amounts directly to candidates; super PACs spend independently and cannot coordinate with campaigns; lobbyists advocate directly to officials
distractors: PACs and super PACs are the same thing and both coordinate with campaigns
Lobbyists donate unlimited sums; PACs may only run advertisements
Super PACs donate directly to candidates; PACs may only lobby
questions.explanation: After Citizens United and related rulings, independent-spending groups (super PACs) may raise and spend unlimited sums but cannot donate to or coordinate with candidates. Traditional PACs accept limited contributions and donate limited amounts directly, and lobbying is direct advocacy aimed at officials - a First Amendment petition activity.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Limited direct gifts, unlimited independent ads, direct advocacy - three lanes.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of three lanes on a civic plaza - one with small donation envelopes, one with a billboard crew, one with a meeting room door. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: PACs give limited direct donations; super PACs spend independently.
img.title: THREE LANES OF INFLUENCE

questions.question: Washington entered the Union and adopted its state constitution in the same year, an event marked by the new state immediately writing a Declaration of Rights as the opening article of its charter. Which year was it?
questions.correctAnswer: 1889 - Washington became the 42nd state and adopted the Washington Constitution
distractors: 1853 - Washington Territory was organized and the constitution was written then
1912 - statehood and the constitution both arrived with the direct-democracy amendments
1846 - the Oregon Treaty set the border and Washington adopted its constitution
questions.explanation: Washington achieved statehood on November 11, 1889, as the 42nd state, and voters ratified the Washington Constitution that same year. The territorial period came earlier, beginning in 1853; direct-democracy amendments arrived more than twenty years after statehood.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Statehood and the state constitution share one year - 1889.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a crowd outside a new domed capitol in 1889 with construction scaffolding still on one wing and flags flying. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Washington statehood and its constitution both date to 1889.
img.title: STATEHOOD AND CONSTITUTION, 1889

questions.question: A student opens the Washington Constitution to find the state's own bill of rights and is told to start at the very beginning of the document. Where are Washington's core individual rights listed?
questions.correctAnswer: Article I, the Declaration of Rights - the opening article of the Washington Constitution
distractors: Article II - the legislative article lists all individual rights
The Preamble alone - Washington has no separate rights article
An appendix added in 1972 - the original document had no rights list
questions.explanation: Article I of the Washington Constitution is its Declaration of Rights, covering subjects such as free speech, religion, due process, jury trial, privacy and the right to bear arms. It stands first in the document, ahead of the articles that build the branches of state government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Washington puts its rights first - Article I, the Declaration of Rights.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of the first page of a large state constitution opened on a reading desk, a bookmark at its opening article. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Article I is Washington's Declaration of Rights.
img.title: RIGHTS COME FIRST

questions.question: Police in Washington search a home in a way lawyers argue violates privacy. The defense insists the state constitution can protect the resident even if the federal charter, as courts read it, would allow the search. Is that argument sound in Washington?
questions.correctAnswer: Yes - Washington courts read Article I independently, and its privacy protection is in places more protective than the federal Fourth Amendment
distractors: No - a state constitution can never protect a right more than the US Constitution does
No - state constitutions apply only to taxes and elections
Yes, but only because Washington judges are elected rather than appointed
questions.explanation: State constitutions set a floor of their own, not a ceiling: the US Constitution guarantees a minimum of rights, and states may protect more. Washington courts have held that Article I, section 7, protecting private affairs from disturbance without authority of law, can be more protective than the Fourth Amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federal rights are the floor - Washington may build higher.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a house at dusk with a glowing shield shape over its roof while a searchlight beam stops at the property line. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Washington's Article I can protect rights beyond the federal floor.
img.title: THE FLOOR, NOT THE CEILING

questions.question: A reader flips between the US Constitution and the Washington Constitution and notices one is a slim framework while the other runs to many times its length, regulating subjects the federal charter never mentions. Which pairing is accurate?
questions.correctAnswer: The Washington Constitution is far longer and more detailed - it reaches subjects such as education, public lands and local government in specific terms
distractors: The US Constitution is longer - it regulates schools and county governments in detail
Both documents are about the same length and cover the same subjects
The Washington Constitution is shorter - it copies the federal text word for word
questions.explanation: The US Constitution is a short framework of roughly seven to eight thousand words. The Washington Constitution is many times longer and far more detailed - it commands a thorough and uniform system of public schools as a paramount duty, governs state lands and debt, and has been amended more than a hundred times.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A framework for the nation, a rulebook for the state.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a slim parchment volume standing beside a very thick bound state code on a library shelf. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Washington's constitution is much longer and more detailed than the federal one.
img.title: FRAMEWORK VERSUS RULEBOOK

questions.question: Frustrated with the legislature, Washington citizens draft a new law themselves, gather signatures, and put the measure on the ballot for voters to enact directly. Which tool of direct democracy are they using?
questions.correctAnswer: The initiative - citizens propose a law and voters enact or reject it at the ballot
distractors: The referendum - the legislature sends its own act to the voters
The recall - voters remove an official before the term ends
The primary - voters choose a party's nominees
questions.explanation: The initiative lets citizens draft legislation, gather the required signatures, and place the measure before the voters (or first before the legislature, depending on the type). Washington voters gained the initiative by constitutional amendment in 1912.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Initiative: citizens write it, voters decide it.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of citizens at a folding table collecting signatures on clipboards outside a public library. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The initiative lets citizens propose laws directly.
img.title: CITIZENS PROPOSE THE LAW

questions.question: The Washington legislature passes a controversial law, and opponents quickly gather signatures to force the law onto the ballot so voters can approve or reject it before it settles in. Which tool are they using?
questions.correctAnswer: The popular referendum - citizens refer a just-passed legislative act to a vote of the people
distractors: The initiative - citizens write an entirely new law from scratch
The recall - citizens remove the legislators who passed the law
The veto - the governor returns the law to the legislature
questions.explanation: The popular referendum lets voters challenge an act the legislature has just passed: gather enough valid signatures within the deadline and the act goes to the ballot, where voters approve or reject it. It is the people's veto over a legislative act, distinct from writing a new law by initiative.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Referendum: the legislature wrote it, the people review it.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of voters reviewing a thick legislative document at a ballot drop box outside a county elections office. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A popular referendum sends a passed law to the voters.
img.title: THE PEOPLE REVIEW THE LAW

questions.question: On a Washington ballot, voters find a measure the legislature itself voted to send to them for a final yes or no, with no citizen signature drive behind it. Which device put it there?
questions.correctAnswer: A legislative referendum - lawmakers referred their own measure to the voters
distractors: A popular referendum - citizens petitioned against a passed law
An initiative - citizens drafted the measure by petition
A recall - voters are deciding whether to remove an official
questions.explanation: Washington knows two kinds of referendum. In a legislative referendum (or referendum bill), the legislature itself refers a measure - often a constitutional amendment or a bond proposal - to the voters for approval. In a popular referendum, citizens force the referral by petition.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Same ballot line, two doors: lawmakers can refer measures too.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of legislators in a domed chamber handing a sealed measure down the steps to waiting voters. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A legislative referendum is referred by the legislature itself.
img.title: LAWMAKERS ASK THE VOTERS

questions.question: Voters in a Washington city collect signatures demanding a special election on whether their mayor should be removed for misconduct, two years before the term expires. Which tool are they using, and what must they show?
questions.correctAnswer: The recall - voters may remove an elected official, and the charges must allege misfeasance, malfeasance or violation of the oath of office
distractors: The initiative - voters may replace any official by passing a law
Impeachment - voters charge the official and the Senate tries the case
The referendum - voters may repeal the election result itself
questions.explanation: Washington's recall, adopted in 1912, lets voters remove elected officials mid-term, but it is not a no-confidence vote: the petition must charge misfeasance, malfeasance or an oath violation, and a court reviews whether the charges are legally sufficient before the election is held.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Recall removes the official - but only for charged misconduct.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of voters signing a petition at a city hall entrance while an official watches from an upper window. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Recall removes officials mid-term for charged misconduct.
img.title: REMOVING AN OFFICIAL MID-TERM

questions.question: Washington's original 1889 constitution gave lawmaking entirely to the legislature. Within a generation, voters had amended it three times to claim direct lawmaking and removal powers for themselves. Which sequence is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: Initiative and referendum were added by amendment in 1912 (with the first initiative measures following), and recall in 1912 as well - all in the 1911-1912 reform wave, alongside the direct primary era changes
distractors: All three tools stood in the original 1889 text unchanged
Initiative arrived in 1889, referendum in 1950 and recall in 2000
The tools were granted by Congress in the statehood act of 1889
questions.explanation: The 1889 constitution contained none of the three devices. Progressive-era voters amended it to add the initiative and referendum in 1912 and the recall in the same reform period (1911-1912) - the same wave that swept direct-democracy reforms across the American West.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1889 built the legislature; 1911-1912 handed voters their own tools.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a 1912 street scene with citizens pinning reform notices on a board outside a county courthouse. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Initiative, referendum and recall came by amendment in 1911-1912.
img.title: THE 1911-1912 REFORM WAVE

questions.question: Two signature drives run in Washington: one for an initiative and one for a popular referendum. A volunteer asks how the signature requirements compare and what they are based on. Which answer is safest and correct?
questions.correctAnswer: Both thresholds are set as a percentage of the votes cast for governor at the last gubernatorial election, and the popular referendum's percentage is lower than the initiative's
distractors: Both require signatures from exactly half of all registered voters
The referendum requires more signatures than the initiative in every case
Neither tool requires signatures - filing a fee alone places a measure on the ballot
questions.explanation: Washington ties both signature thresholds to turnout in the governor's race: each is a set percentage of the votes cast for governor at the most recent gubernatorial election, and the popular referendum's percentage is lower than the initiative's - which fits its role as a quick check on a law just passed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Thresholds ride on the governor's race - and the referendum bar sits lower.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two stacks of signed petition sheets on a table, one stack visibly taller than the other, beside a ballot box. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Both thresholds are percentages of the last governor's vote; the referendum's is lower.
img.title: PERCENTAGES OF THE GOVERNOR'S RACE

questions.question: A civics class reads that the tribes within Washington's borders are not clubs, counties or federal agencies, and that the state cannot simply legislate over them. What status explains that limit?
questions.correctAnswer: Tribal sovereignty - federally recognized tribes are sovereign governments whose authority predates the United States
distractors: Home rule - tribes govern only what a city charter allows
Special-district status - tribes operate as units of county government
Federal employment status - tribal councils are agencies of the state
questions.explanation: Federally recognized tribes are sovereign political communities: their governing authority is inherent and predates the US Constitution, and their relationship runs government-to-government with the United States. Washington contains 29 federally recognized tribes, each with its own government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tribes are governments, not interest groups or agencies.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a tribal council building with a tribal flag flying beside a river at dawn, mountains behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Tribes are sovereign governments with inherent authority.
img.title: SOVEREIGN SINCE TIME IMMEMORIAL

questions.question: A state agency plans a policy affecting treaty fishing and consults a tribal government as one government meeting another, not as a stakeholder to be notified afterward. Which principle and which Washington agreement frame that duty?
questions.correctAnswer: Government-to-government relations - formalized for Washington by the 1989 Centennial Accord between the state and the tribes
distractors: The Origination Clause - revenue measures begin the consultation
The Centennial Accord of 1889 - signed at statehood by the territorial governor
Home rule - cities and tribes exchange services by charter
questions.explanation: In 1989 - the centennial of statehood - Washington and the federally recognized tribes signed the Centennial Accord, committing the state to government-to-government relations with each tribe. Consultation with tribal governments follows from their sovereign status, not from public-comment courtesy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1989: one hundred years in, the state pledged government-to-government dealing.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of state and tribal leaders seated as equals at one long table with two flags standing side by side. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The 1989 Centennial Accord frames government-to-government relations.
img.title: THE CENTENNIAL ACCORD, 1989

questions.question: In the 1850s, a territorial governor signed treaties in which tribes gave up vast lands but kept the right to fish at their usual and accustomed places. A century later, a federal judge enforced that promise. What did the Boldt decision (1974) hold?
questions.correctAnswer: The treaty language reserved real fishing rights - treaty tribes were entitled to up to half the harvestable fish, with the treaties read as the tribes would have understood them
distractors: The treaties were ceremonial and reserved no enforceable rights
Fishing rights ended automatically at statehood in 1889
The state could regulate treaty fishing exactly like all other fishing with no treaty limit
questions.explanation: In United States v. Washington (1974), Judge George Boldt held that the Stevens treaties of 1854-1855 reserved the tribes' right to take fish at their usual and accustomed grounds, entitling treaty tribes to up to half of the harvestable catch. The US Supreme Court largely affirmed the ruling, and co-management of the fishery followed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Reserved rights are rights kept, not rights granted.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of salmon leaping in a river below a bridge while tribal fishers and state biologists review charts on the bank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Boldt (1974): treaties reserved up to half the harvestable fish.
img.title: RIGHTS KEPT, NOT GRANTED

questions.question: A student asks why treaty promises made by the United States to tribes in the 1850s still bind Washington today, when the state did not sign them. Which answer is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: Treaties are part of the supreme law of the land under the US Constitution, and Washington entered the Union subject to them - a state cannot erase federal treaty obligations
distractors: They bind only as a courtesy that each legislature may end at will
They expired when the territorial government became a state
They bind because the Washington Constitution copied them word for word
questions.explanation: Article VI makes treaties made under US authority part of the supreme law of the land. The treaties with Washington tribes were federal agreements, so statehood did not cancel them; Washington's own enabling terms also disclaimed state control over tribal lands and recognized federal authority.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A treaty outranks a state's wish to forget it - supremacy again.

questions.question: Washington's legislature has two chambers elected from the same map: every district elects one senator and two representatives. How many legislative districts does Washington have?
questions.correctAnswer: 49 legislative districts, each sending one senator and two representatives to Olympia
distractors: 10 legislative districts, matching the congressional map
39 legislative districts, one for every county
98 legislative districts, one for every representative
questions.explanation: Washington is divided into 49 legislative districts of roughly equal population, redrawn after each census by a bipartisan redistricting commission. Each district elects one of the 49 senators and two of the 98 representatives.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 49 districts, three legislators each - one senator, two representatives.

questions.question: A Washington state senator wins election and will not face the voters again for a full presidential term cycle, while her House seatmates return to the ballot every two years. Which numbers describe the two chambers?
questions.correctAnswer: 49 senators serving four-year terms; 98 representatives serving two-year terms
distractors: 49 senators serving two-year terms; 98 representatives serving four-year terms
50 senators serving six-year terms; 100 representatives serving two-year terms
39 senators serving four-year terms; 78 representatives serving two-year terms
questions.explanation: The Washington Senate has 49 members, one per district, serving staggered four-year terms. The state House of Representatives has 98 members, two per district, all elected every two years - the same two-per-district pattern repeated statewide.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Senate: 49 and four years. House: 98 and two years.

questions.question: A bill passes the Washington Senate and House and reaches the governor, who supports most of it but objects to specific spending lines in the budget bill. What can the Washington governor do that the US President cannot?
questions.correctAnswer: Exercise a partial (section) veto - Washington's governor may veto individual sections or items of a bill, especially in appropriations, while the rest becomes law
distractors: Rewrite the bill's text and enact the rewritten version directly
Send the bill to the voters as a mandatory referendum
Order the state supreme court to review the bill before signing
questions.explanation: Washington's governor holds one of the nation's stronger veto pens: the state constitution allows vetoing a section or sections of a bill, and appropriation items, without killing the whole measure. The federal President must sign or veto a bill entire - the US Supreme Court struck down the federal line-item veto.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Washington's governor can veto a section and sign the rest.

img.tip: Washington's governor has a section veto the President lacks.

questions.question: A naturalization applicant living in Washington is asked to name the capital of her state - the city where the legislature meets and the governor works. Which answer is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: Olympia
distractors: Seattle
Spokane
Tacoma
questions.explanation: Olympia, at the south end of Puget Sound, has been Washington's capital since territorial days and is home to the state capitol campus, the legislature and the governor's office. Seattle is the state's largest city but not its capital.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The capital is Olympia - the biggest city is not the capital.

questions.question: A Washington voter marks separate ballot choices for governor, lieutenant governor, secretary of state, attorney general, treasurer, auditor, superintendent of public instruction, commissioner of public lands and insurance commissioner. What is this arrangement called, and why does it matter?
questions.correctAnswer: A plural executive - voters separately elect nine statewide executives, so the governor cannot appoint or remove most of them
distractors: A unitary executive - the governor appoints every statewide officer
A cabinet system - the legislature elects all nine officers
A commission government - the nine officers share the governorship equally
questions.explanation: Unlike the federal executive, where the President appoints the Cabinet, Washington divides executive power among nine separately elected officials. Each answers to the voters directly, so a governor cannot fire an attorney general or treasurer who disagrees - the design trades unified control for independent accountability.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nine executives, nine separate elections - the governor hires none of them.

img.tip: Washington has a plural executive of nine elected officials.

questions.question: Match the job to the office: the state's chief elections officer who also keeps state records; the state's chief legal officer who represents Washington in court; the elected head of the public school system. Which offices, in order?
questions.correctAnswer: Secretary of State; Attorney General; Superintendent of Public Instruction
distractors: Treasurer; Auditor; Commissioner of Public Lands
Insurance Commissioner; Lieutenant Governor; Treasurer
Attorney General; Secretary of State; Governor
questions.explanation: Washington's separately elected executives divide the work: the Secretary of State is the chief elections officer and custodian of state records, the Attorney General is the state's chief legal officer, and the Superintendent of Public Instruction heads the state school system (OSPI). The Treasurer, Auditor, Commissioner of Public Lands and Insurance Commissioner are likewise elected on their own.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Elections: Secretary of State. Law: Attorney General. Schools: the Superintendent.

questions.question: Washington's governor is elected statewide, serves as the state's chief executive, commands the state National Guard, proposes a budget and signs or vetoes bills. How long is one term, and how many terms may a governor serve?
questions.correctAnswer: Four-year terms, with no constitutional limit on the number of terms
distractors: Two-year terms, limited to two terms by the constitution
Six-year terms, limited to one term by the constitution
Four-year terms, limited to two terms by the 22nd Amendment
questions.explanation: Washington governors serve four-year terms and the state constitution sets no term limit on the office - unlike the US President, capped at two elected terms by the 22nd Amendment. Washington voters have in fact returned governors for third terms.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Four years a term - and no state cap on how many.

questions.question: One Washington executive is elected to manage millions of acres of state trust lands - forests, farmland and aquatic lands whose income supports public schools and other public institutions - and leads the agency that manages them. Which office is it?
questions.correctAnswer: The Commissioner of Public Lands, who heads the Department of Natural Resources
distractors: The State Treasurer, who heads the Department of Revenue
The State Auditor, who heads the Department of Ecology
The Insurance Commissioner, who heads the Parks Commission
questions.explanation: The Commissioner of Public Lands, one of Washington's nine elected executives, leads the Department of Natural Resources. The office manages state trust lands whose timber, leases and other income benefit public schools and universities - a duty written into the state constitution at statehood.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Trust lands pay for schools - the Lands Commissioner manages them.

questions.question: A Washington supreme court justice finishes a campaign in which voters statewide chose among candidates without party labels on the ballot. How many justices sit on the state's highest court, and how long is a term?
questions.correctAnswer: Nine justices, elected statewide to six-year terms in nonpartisan elections
distractors: Seven justices, appointed by the governor for life
Nine justices, appointed by the legislature to four-year terms
Five justices, elected by district to two-year terms
questions.explanation: The Washington Supreme Court has nine justices, elected statewide in nonpartisan elections to staggered six-year terms - a sharp contrast with the US Supreme Court, whose nine members are appointed and serve for life. The court sits in Olympia and is the final word on Washington law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: State justices: elected, six years. Federal justices: appointed, for life.

questions.question: A felony trial, a major civil suit and a family-law case all begin in the same kind of Washington court, while a mid-sized appeal from that court goes one level up before reaching the state supreme court. Which structure is this?
questions.correctAnswer: Superior courts are the trial courts of general jurisdiction in every county; the Court of Appeals is the intermediate appellate court; the state supreme court sits at the top
distractors: District courts try all felonies; municipal courts hear all appeals; the supreme court tries cases first
The Court of Appeals tries felonies; superior courts hear only appeals
All cases begin in the state supreme court and are assigned downward
questions.explanation: Washington's court ladder mirrors the federal one with elected judges: superior courts, present in all 39 counties, are the general trial courts for felonies and major civil cases; the Court of Appeals, in three divisions, reviews most appeals; and the Washington Supreme Court reviews last. Below superior court sit district and municipal courts of limited jurisdiction.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Superior tries, Appeals reviews, Supreme decides last.

questions.question: Washington's counties run elections, record property, maintain roads and provide sheriffs and courts across the whole state, including its largest county, King, and small rural counties. How many counties does Washington have?
questions.correctAnswer: 39 counties
distractors: 29 counties
49 counties
58 counties
questions.explanation: Washington has 39 counties, from King County (Seattle) to small counties such as Garfield and Wahkiakum. Each county elects officials including commissioners or a council, a sheriff, a prosecutor and an assessor, and counties serve as the state's arm for elections, records and courts.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 39 counties carry the state's daily work.

questions.question: A Washington family gets drinking water from a public utility district, fire protection from a fire district, schooling from a school district and port services from a port district - none of them run by the city or county. What are these governments?
questions.correctAnswer: Special purpose districts - single-function local governments created under state law to deliver one service
distractors: Federal agencies assigned to the neighborhood
Private companies that voters may not tax or govern
Tribal governments serving their enrolled citizens
questions.explanation: Washington is covered by well over a thousand special purpose districts - school, fire, water, sewer, port, hospital and public utility districts among them. Each is a separate local government, usually with its own elected board and taxing or rate authority, created to deliver one service across whatever boundaries fit that service.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One service, one district, one elected board.

questions.question: In Washington's primary, a voter sees candidates of several parties for one office on a single ballot, and the same two names - sometimes from the same party - appear again in November. Which system produces that result?
questions.correctAnswer: The Top 2 primary - the two candidates with the most primary votes advance to the general election regardless of party
distractors: A closed party primary - each party advances its own nominee to November
A runoff system - the legislature picks the final two candidates
Proportional representation - parties advance in proportion to their vote
questions.explanation: Washington voters adopted the Top 2 primary by initiative in 2004, and the US Supreme Court upheld it. Every voter uses one ballot, candidates state a party preference, and the top two finishers meet in the general election - which can pair two candidates who prefer the same party. It does not apply to presidential races, which use a separate presidential primary.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Top 2: the ballot does not ask your party - the top two advance.

questions.question: A Washington voter's ballot arrives at her home weeks before an election; she marks it at her kitchen table and returns it through the mail or an official drop box by Election Day. Which system is she using?
questions.correctAnswer: Vote-by-mail - Washington conducts elections by mail, sending a ballot to every registered voter
distractors: Precinct-only voting - ballots exist only inside a polling place
Caucus voting - neighbors gather to choose in public
Absentee-only voting - mail ballots require a documented excuse
questions.explanation: Washington runs its elections primarily by mail: every registered voter is mailed a ballot, and counties provide drop boxes and in-person voting centers as backups. No excuse is needed - mail voting is the default method, adopted statewide after counties had already moved most voting to the mail.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The ballot comes to the voter - mail is the default.

questions.question: A new Washington resident realizes on Election Day itself that she never registered. A friend says it is too late - registration closed weeks ago. Who is right under current Washington law?
questions.correctAnswer: The friend is wrong - Washington allows same-day registration in person at a county voting center up to and including Election Day
distractors: The friend is right - Washington registration closes 30 days before every election with no exceptions
The resident may vote only if a registered voter vouches for her in writing
The resident may register on Election Day only for presidential elections
questions.explanation: Washington modernized registration in steps: online and mail registration close about eight days before an election, but in-person registration at a county elections office or voting center stays open through Election Day itself. Same-day registration means moving or forgetting does not cost a qualified voter the ballot.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Forgot to register? In person, through Election Day, still counts.

questions.question: A 16-year-old in Tacoma fills out a voter registration form at her licensing office even though she cannot vote yet, and her registration will activate when she turns 18. Which Washington program is she using?
questions.correctAnswer: The Future Voter program - 16- and 17-year-olds may pre-register and are automatically registered when they become eligible
distractors: The youth ballot program - 16-year-olds vote in school elections only
The junior elector program - teens cast provisional ballots that are counted at 18
The early registration ban - the form will be discarded as invalid
questions.explanation: Washington's Future Voter program lets 16- and 17-year-olds pre-register - at licensing offices, by mail, online and in school programs - and the registration takes effect automatically when they turn 18, with a first ballot following at the next election. Pre-registration is meant to make registration a habit before the first eligible election.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sign up at 16, vote at 18 - the registration waits for you.
